title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d,C',e\) with the following guarantee for every \(m,n\ge1\), \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb Q^m\) and \(c\in\mathbb Q^n\)? For the linear program
\[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x: x\in\mathbb R^n,\ Ax=b,\ x\ge0\},\]
the algorithm returns an exact rational optimal vector, or correctly reports infeasibility or an objective unbounded below. It uses at most \(C(m+n+1)^d\) elementary operations in the rational arithmetic model below, and every numerical value during the computation has binary encoding length at most \(C'(N+1)^e\), where \(N\) is the full input bit length. The same program and constants must work for all dimensions and coefficient values.
definitions:
The input contains the dimensions and the complete dense lists of entries of \(A,b,c\), including zeros. Each rational is supplied as a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. Their lengths, the dimensions and the delimiters all contribute to \(N\). No rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, boundedness, coefficient-size or conditioning promise is imposed. The variables range over the real numbers; rational input guarantees that a finite optimum, when the feasible set is nonempty and the objective bounded below, has a rational optimal vector.

Computation uses one fixed finite arithmetic-RAM program with rational registers, integer addresses and finite control. One scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational, exact comparison, register read/write or copy costs one operation. Conditional branches, elementary integer index arithmetic and comparisons, and data transfers also count. Index operations are integer addition and subtraction; indirect addressing accesses one location at a time. Indices start from dimensions or fixed integer constants and are manipulated by these index operations. A rational coefficient or computed rational cannot be reinterpreted as an address. Each scalar entry of a vector or matrix operation must be charged separately. All preprocessing, memory access, feasibility testing and production of the output count. A scalar rational input read or output write counts once at this arithmetic level; transferring its individual binary digits is accounted for by the bit implementation.

The program may contain finitely many fixed rational constants. It has no oracle, advice, randomness, floor or integer-part primitive, square-root primitive, or instruction inspecting the binary digits, numerator, denominator or encoding length of a rational register. Comparisons and arithmetic act on exact rational values, not floating-point approximations. Here the binary size of a rational is the combined length of its signed numerator and positive denominator in lowest terms. The bound also covers integer indices and the output. Reduction to lowest terms specifies representation and exact bit simulation; it supplies no additional operation with which the arithmetic program can extract numerator or denominator data. The elementary rational operations must admit an exact implementation on a binary multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in their operand lengths. Thus the dimension-only operation bound together with the polynomial numerical-size bound yields total bit time polynomial in \(N\); the bit-time bound is not required to be independent of \(N\).

Let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\). An infeasibility answer is correct exactly when \(F=\varnothing\). An unbounded-below answer is correct exactly when \(F\ne\varnothing\) and
\[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists x\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x<M.\]
Otherwise the algorithm must return \(x^*\in F\cap\mathbb Q^n\) with
\[\forall y\in F,\qquad c^{\mathsf T}x^*\le c^{\mathsf T}y.\]
Any optimal vector is allowed when several exist; an optimal basis is not required. An unbounded feasible region can still have a finite minimum, and must then receive an optimal-vector output. Infeasibility and unboundedness outputs are distinct tags, not an approximate numerical infinity. The operation bound depends only on \(m+n\); neither coefficient magnitudes, their bit lengths, numerical conditioning nor a requested accuracy may enter it.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of this algorithm-existence statement or of its logical negation. A positive answer must specify a finite deterministic program, prove its correct exact output in all three cases for every rational input, and prove both a single dimension-only polynomial operation bound and a single polynomial bound on numerical encoding lengths, with an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.

A negative answer must prove that no program with any fixed constants \(C,d,C',e\) satisfies all these requirements on every input. An exponential example for one pivot rule or a restricted class of interior-point methods does not exclude every algorithm in the specified model. A guarantee restricted to special matrices, fixed dimension, well-conditioned or strictly feasible inputs, or an approximate optimum does not settle the question. This is a yes/no existence target; the benchmark's numerical approximation tolerance does not replace exact optimization or either complexity bound.
why: Linear programming is a basic language for optimization across combinatorics, algorithms and applications. The question asks whether exact optimization needs a number of arithmetic decisions that grows with numerical precision, or whether the dimensions alone suffice. A positive answer would extend a central efficiency property of several combinatorial optimization problems to every rational linear program.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: Tardos establishes arithmetic bounds independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix.
Exponential iteration lower bounds apply to the stated central-path neighborhood framework, not to all LP algorithms.
The STOC theorem gives a deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm for minimum-cost generalized flow and the two-nonzero-per-row-or-column classes, with a Turing-model implementation.
The STOC 2026 trust-region work improves path-following bounds relative to neighborhood straight-line complexity; it does not assert a dimension-only bound for arbitrary LP.
Awoniyi’s version 10 retains a general solution claim; its proof has not been independently certified by this review.
Truffet’s version 4 states a general solution claim and describes a correction to earlier versions. Its source PDF is internally dated 1 September 2026.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The established 2024 and 2026 primary results inspected here retain special-matrix or path-complexity/model qualifications. Awoniyi’s current v10 and Truffet’s current v4 directly claim general strongly polynomial LP algorithms; their proofs and the complete card requirements have not been independently certified by this review. Awoniyi’s separate Validation preprint is by the same author. Truffet’s current version acknowledges and asserts correction of an earlier logical error. Bounded searches did not establish independent primary validation of either full claim, so the card remains uncertain and active. This is not an exhaustive proof audit.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms polynomial in the full binary input length. That length can increase while the numbers of variables and constraints stay fixed. Strong polynomiality asks for a dimension-only arithmetic operation count while retaining polynomially bounded numerical representations. It does not promise that writing an arbitrarily long exact output takes a constant number of bit operations.

The three output cases refer to the objective as well as the feasible set. For example, \(x_1=1\), \(x_2\ge0\), with objective \(x_1\), has an unbounded feasible region and finite minimum \(1\). The algorithm must return an optimal vector in this case. Failure to find a feasible point is not by itself a certificate that none exists.

Tardos’s 1986 theorem removes the dependence of the arithmetic operation count on the right-hand side and objective coefficients, while retaining dependence on the constraint matrix. This gives strong polynomiality for important small-coefficient matrix classes. Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver and Végh’s STOC 2024 theorem covers minimum-cost generalized flow and linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or per column, including controlled bit complexity. An unrestricted dense matrix need not belong to these classes.

Allamigeon, Gaubert and Vandame prove exponential iteration lower bounds for interior-point trajectories confined to the specified neighborhoods of self-concordant-barrier central paths. A central path is the curve of minimizers of the barrier-penalized objective as its parameter varies. Their theorem restricts which trajectories the method follows; it is not a lower bound for every arithmetic algorithm for linear programming.

The STOC 2026 trust-region paper gives guarantees relative to the straight-line complexity of an appropriate central-path neighborhood: the number of line segments needed to traverse it. Instance optimality within this path-following framework does not supply a dimension-only polynomial bound on that quantity for every LP. The paper also distinguishes its real-RAM running times from the additional work needed to control bit complexity. Its approximate trust-region subproblems retain accuracy parameters and are not exact general LP solvers.

Awoniyi’s July 2026 revision directly claims a strongly polynomial algorithm for general LP; Lemma 7.1 asserts a linear bound on its iteration count. A separate paper entitled Validation is by the same author, so its title does not establish independent confirmation. This review has not certified the proof or located independent primary validation in bounded searches.

Truffet’s current August 2026 revision also states a general strongly polynomial solution in Theorem 2.1. Its opening revision note acknowledges a logical error in earlier versions and asserts a correction; the current theorem remains a claim requiring verification. This review read that note, the theorem and the stated complexity conclusion, without certifying their proof or the full bit-complexity requirements. These unresolved claims are why the card retains uncertain status.

sentences: A rational linear program minimizes a linear objective subject to linear equalities and nonnegative variables.
The question asks for one deterministic exact solver using polynomially many scalar arithmetic operations depending only on the numbers of variables and constraints.
Intermediate rational values must have bit lengths polynomial in the full input length, and the computation must admit an exact polynomial-time bit implementation.
The solver must distinguish infeasibility, an objective unbounded below and a finite attained optimum on every input, without matrix or conditioning promises.
Strongly polynomial algorithms are established for major special classes, while current claims of a general solution remain unverified in this review.

source_formulation.text: The Open Problems Project asks whether linear programming is strongly polynomial. This card retains its previously selected deterministic rational-input, exact-output formulation. The explicit scalar arithmetic and binary-size conventions fix the rational arithmetic/Turing variant discussed in Section 1.3 of the STOC 2024 paper; the card measures rational values in lowest terms and separately requires polynomial bit simulation. The paper additionally proves its special-case result under a stricter unreduced numerator-denominator representation convention. Neither that stronger representation result nor the arbitrary-real BSS formulation is silently substituted for this card’s retained target.
